title: Sex and the Body: A Theology of Desire
subtitle: The body is good, desire is good, and both were made to mean something. A frank and serious Christian reckoning with sex, chastity, and longing, against both the prudery that fears the body and the license that wastes it.

parts.title: The Thing the Church Will Not Talk About
parts.body:
You learned about sex from everywhere except the people who should have taught you. From the schoolyard, the screen, the magazine, the older kid who knew things, the algorithm that learned your loneliness and fed it. And from the church, if the church said anything at all, you mostly learned a single word, no, delivered with enough fear and shame attached that the topic itself came to feel dirty, as though the desire in your own body were an enemy to be ashamed of rather than a gift to be understood. So you grew up split, your faith on one side and your body on the other, and the silence between them did far more damage than any honest conversation ever could.

For some of us the struggle is the wound of that shame. We absorbed the message that the body is suspect and desire is dangerous, and we carried it into marriage where it did not magically dissolve at the altar, so that the very thing Scripture calls good still feels, somewhere below conscious thought, like something to apologize for. For some of us the struggle is the opposite, the long slow surrender to a culture that treats sex as recreation and the body as a tool for pleasure, and we have followed that road far enough to feel the emptiness it leaves, the bodies used and discarded, our own among them, the strange loneliness of intimacy without covenant.

For many of us the struggle is the screen, the endless, frictionless, private availability of bodies on demand, a habit formed before we understood what it was forming, a counterfeit that has rewired desire and isolated us in the very act that was made for union. We hate it and we return to it. We confess it and we hide it. And the shame keeps it in the dark, where it grows, because we have never once heard it spoken about in church as anything but a sin too embarrassing to name.

And for some of us, the struggle is simply longing. The single years that stretch longer than anyone promised. The desire that has no covenant to flow into, the ache the church often pretends does not exist, the lonely question of what to do with a good gift and no place to give it. If that is you, hear this first, before anything else. Your desire is not your shame, your singleness is not your failure, and the body that aches is not a problem to be solved but a good thing waiting, and the church that has had nothing to say to you but wait has failed you.

Let me be as plain and as serious as Scripture itself is, which is more frank about the body than most sermons dare to be. The Song of Songs is in the Bible, eight chapters of unembarrassed erotic poetry, and God put it there on purpose. The body is good. Desire is good. Sex is good, a gift from the God who invented it and called the whole material world very good. The problem was never the desire. The problem is that we have lost the meaning of it, caught between a church that feared the gift and a culture that wasted it, and almost no one has told us the truth, that the body means something, that desire was made to point somewhere, and that the recovery of its meaning is the recovery of joy.

parts.title: Why the Body Means Something
parts.body:
It matters because the body is not a costume you wear or a vehicle you drive. It is you. The oldest heresy the church ever fought was the lie that the real self is a soul trapped in an irrelevant lump of matter, and we have rebuilt that heresy in two opposite forms, the prudery that treats the body as a shameful thing to be subdued and the license that treats it as a meaningless thing to be used. Both deny the same truth, that what you do with your body, you do with yourself, that there is no such thing as merely physical, and that sex, of all bodily acts, is the one Scripture insists touches the deepest part of a person.

It matters because sex is never only physical, however hard the culture works to convince you it is. Paul looked at the Corinthians treating sex as a bodily transaction with no more weight than a meal, and he refused the premise outright. Do you not know, he asks, that the two become one flesh, that the body is not made for sexual immorality but for the Lord. Sex enacts a union whether or not the participants intend one, joins selves whether or not they meant to be joined, and this is why its misuse wounds in a way that other appetites do not. You can eat a meal and walk away unchanged. You cannot give your body to someone and walk away unchanged, because the body is not separable from the self. The casual sex the culture sells is sold on a lie, that you can do this thing and it will mean nothing, and the loneliness and the wounds it leaves are the truth breaking through the lie.

It matters because a whole generation is being discipled in a theology of the body by the screen, and it is a brutal one. Pornography teaches, with relentless repetition, that bodies are for consumption, that the other person is a means to your pleasure, that desire is satisfied by taking rather than by giving, and that intimacy can be had without covenant, without cost, without the inconvenient presence of an actual person. It rewires the very machinery of desire toward isolation, training a person to want a image rather than a beloved, and it leaves its users lonelier than it found them. This is not a minor vice to be winked at. It is a catechism, and it is forming souls, and the church's embarrassed silence has handed the teaching of an entire generation over to it.

And it matters because how we treat the body and its desires is one of the sharpest places the watching world reads our faith. The skeptic sees a church that often seemed obsessed with sexual sin while ignoring greed and pride, that shamed the desire it could not discuss, that produced as much hidden brokenness as the culture it condemned. He is right to be unimpressed by hypocrisy. But he has rarely seen the actual Christian vision, the claim that the body is so good and so meaningful that it must not be wasted, that desire is so powerful that it deserves a covenant worthy of it, that chastity is not the fear of sex but the reverence for it. A church that recovered that vision, frank and joyful and unashamed, would have something to say that the exhausted, used, lonely children of the sexual revolution have never heard.

parts.title: What Scripture Actually Says About the Body and Desire
parts.body:
Begin where the Bible begins, with a God who makes physical things and calls them good. The opening page of Genesis is a hymn to materiality, light and water and land and bodies, and over each God pronounces the verdict, good, and over the whole, including the embodied human creature made male and female, very good. There is no hint here that matter is lower than spirit, that the body is a problem, that desire is suspect. God made the body. God made the difference and attraction between the sexes. God looked at all of it, naked and unashamed in the garden, and called it very good. Whatever has gone wrong with sex, it did not start with God thinking the body was a mistake.

Then comes the first command about the body and its union, and it is not a prohibition but a design. Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. Notice the architecture. Leaving, holding fast, becoming one flesh, the public reordering of life, the lifelong faithfulness, and then the bodily union, in that order, each part holding the others. Sex in Scripture is the sign and seal of a covenant, the act that means something precisely because it is the bodily enactment of a promise, two persons giving themselves wholly to each other within a bond meant to last. The one-flesh union is not a technique or a transaction. It is a covenant spoken in the language of bodies.

Then, lest anyone imagine the Bible is grudging about the pleasure of it, there is the Song of Songs, eight chapters of frank erotic poetry that the church has spent centuries trying to spiritualize into something safer. Read it plainly and it will not let you. Two lovers praise each other's bodies in vivid and unembarrassed detail, the lover delighting in his beloved, the beloved calling him to her, the whole poem a celebration of desire fulfilled within love. Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, it begins, and it does not get more demure from there. God put a book of love poetry in the canon, a book with no obvious moral lesson and no mention of his own name, simply to say that the delight of two lovers in each other's bodies is good, is blessed, is worthy of a place in holy Scripture. The God who fears the body did not write the Song of Songs. The God who made it and called it good did.

Then comes the realism, because Scripture is honest about how the good gift gets twisted. The same Bible that celebrates desire warns relentlessly against its misuse, not because desire is bad but because a good and powerful thing aimed wrong does terrible damage. Proverbs spends whole chapters steering a young man away from the seduction that ends in poverty and death, and then, in the same breath, turns and commands him to delight in the wife of his youth, to be intoxicated always in her love. There is the whole biblical posture in two movements, refusing both the prudery that fears desire and the folly that wastes it. The commandment against adultery, the warnings against fornication, the call to flee sexual immorality, none of these are God begrudging you pleasure. They are God protecting a gift so powerful it can either build a life or burn it down, fencing the fire so it warms the house instead of consuming it.

Then Jesus, who deepens the whole thing by moving it from behavior to the heart. You have heard it said do not commit adultery, but I say to you that whoever looks at a woman with lust has already committed adultery in his heart. He is not adding cruelty to the law. He is exposing that the issue was never only the act but the orientation of desire itself, the difference between looking at a person as a beloved to be cherished and looking at them as a body to be consumed. And he does this as the one who befriended the woman caught in adultery without condemning her and without excusing her, who said go and sin no more, holding grace and truth together in a single sentence the way no one before him had. Jesus is neither the prude nor the libertine. He is the one who takes both the body and the desire so seriously that he will not let either be wasted.

Then Paul, who gives the gift its deepest meaning and its highest dignity. He tells the Corinthians that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, bought with a price, and therefore not their own to use however they wish. And then, astonishingly, he takes the one-flesh union of husband and wife and says it points beyond itself, that this mystery is profound, and he is saying it refers to Christ and the church. The union of two bodies in covenant love is an icon, a living sign, of the union between Christ and his people, the self-giving love of God made visible in flesh. Which means that sex, rightly understood, is not less than the culture thinks. It is infinitely more. It is a sacrament of the love that made the universe and gave itself away on a cross. No wonder it cannot be casual. It was always pointing at the deepest thing there is.

parts.title: The Church and the Body, the Glory and the Failure
parts.body:
The church's history with the body is a story of both profound wisdom and real failure, and honesty requires telling both. In its first centuries the church fought, and won, a war over the goodness of matter itself. The great heresy was Gnosticism, which taught that the physical world was a prison, the body a thing to escape, and salvation a flight of the pure soul out of corrupt matter. Against it the church planted its flag on the most physical claims imaginable, that God made the world and called it good, that the Word became flesh and was born from a woman's body, that Christ was raised bodily from the dead and his followers would be too. The Apostles' Creed ends not with the immortality of the soul but with the resurrection of the body, a deliberate refusal of every spirituality that despises the flesh. The church that confesses that creed cannot, in principle, hold the body in contempt.

And yet the contempt crept in anyway, through a different door. Influenced more by the Greek philosophers than by the Hebrew Scriptures, some of the early teachers came to treat sexual desire itself as the great enemy, virginity as the highest state, and marriage as a grudging concession to weakness. Augustine, brilliant and tormented by his own past, taught that the desire itself was tainted by sin, and his enormous influence bent the Western church toward a suspicion of sexuality that the Song of Songs should have prevented. The medieval church often spoke of sex within marriage as permissible only for procreation, the pleasure a regrettable necessity, and the long shadow of that error is the prudery many of us inherited, the sense that the body is suspect and desire is shameful, which is not the teaching of Scripture but a distortion that Scripture itself rebukes.

The Reformation brought a needed recovery. Martin Luther, who left the monastery and married a former nun, Katharina von Bora, taught loudly that marriage was not a lower estate but a holy calling, that sexual love within it was a good gift of God, and that the celibacy demanded of priests had often produced more hidden sin than holiness. The Reformers restored the dignity of marriage and the goodness of the marriage bed, and the Puritans, despite the dour reputation history has unfairly hung on them, wrote some of the warmest counsel on married love ever produced, insisting that husbands and wives owe each other delight and that a cold marriage bed was a sin against the covenant. The recovery was real, if incomplete.

And then came the modern revolution, which threw out the prudery and the meaning together. The sexual revolution of the twentieth century, powered by the contraceptive pill in the 1960s and the collapse of the older social structures, made a promise the church had failed to make plausible, that sex could be free, pleasurable, and consequence-free, severed at last from covenant, from children, from permanence, from meaning. It was sold as liberation, and for a time it felt like one. But the bill came due, in the wreckage of broken homes, in a generation of children raised in the rubble of their parents' freedom, in the epidemic of loneliness that followed the promise of endless intimacy, in the rise of a pornography industry that industrialized the consumption of human bodies. The revolution kept its promise to free sex from meaning, and the freedom turned out to be a desert. We are living in its aftermath now, surrounded by people who were told that the body means nothing and are quietly dying of the lie.

And into that aftermath, in the late twentieth century, came one of the church's most important recoveries, the body of teaching that came to be called a theology of the body, which insisted that the body itself has a meaning, that it is made for self-giving love, that the union of the sexes is an icon of divine love, and that chastity is not the repression of desire but its right ordering toward the covenant it was made for. It was the Song of Songs and the goodness of creation and the dignity of the body recovered together, against both the old prudery and the new license, and it remains the most hopeful word the church has spoken on the subject in centuries. The body means something. Desire points somewhere. The recovery of that truth is the recovery of the gift.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: Christians have nothing to fear from honest study of sex, desire, attachment, and the body, because all truth is God's truth, and the research keeps confirming what Scripture assumed, that the body and its bonds mean far more than the culture pretends. We read this work with gratitude and without surprise, and then we test it, because measuring what sex does to a person is not the same as knowing what sex is for. What follows takes five bodies of secular knowledge seriously and tests each against Scripture.

secular.source: The research on attachment and the neurochemistry of bonding
secular.author: Helen Fisher and the science of love and pair-bonding
secular.whatItGetsRight: Fisher and the researchers of human bonding have shown that sex is anything but casual at the level of the body itself, that the act floods the brain with oxytocin and vasopressin and dopamine, the very chemistry of attachment and trust, literally bonding partners to each other whether or not they intend to be bonded. The science demonstrates that the human creature is built to attach through sex, that the body forms a bond the mind may not have consented to, and that the idea of consequence-free, no-strings intimacy runs directly against our own neurochemistry.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The laboratory has stumbled onto Genesis. The two shall become one flesh is not poetry the body can ignore, and the chemistry of bonding is the physical signature of a union Scripture named three thousand years ago. But the science can only describe the mechanism and stops there, treating attachment as a biochemical event to be understood and perhaps managed. Scripture says the bonding means something, that it is the body enacting a covenant, the sign of a self-giving meant to be permanent. The neurochemistry can tell you that casual sex is a lie your body does not believe. Only Scripture can tell you what the truth was for, the covenant love of which the bond is the living seal.

secular.source: The data on pornography and the brain
secular.author: Gary Wilson and the researchers of compulsive sexual behavior
secular.whatItGetsRight: A growing body of research documents that habitual pornography use can reshape the reward circuitry of the brain along the lines of other compulsive behaviors, escalating tolerance, dulling response to real partners, and fostering isolation and dissatisfaction. The science increasingly confirms what users report, that the habit trains desire toward novelty and image rather than persons, that it can damage real intimacy, and that it leaves its users lonelier and less satisfied rather than more.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Scripture saw the deeper shape of this long before the brain scans. Jesus warned that to look with lust is already to have committed adultery in the heart, naming the real damage as the corruption of desire itself, the training of the heart to consume rather than to love. The research can map the rewired circuitry and recommend abstinence as a path to better functioning. Scripture goes deeper, naming the wound as a sin against the body that is a temple and against the person reduced to an image, and offering not only the breaking of a habit but the redemption of desire, the slow reordering of a heart back toward the love it was made for. The data can show you the cage. Only grace can open it.

secular.source: The studies on cohabitation, hookup culture, and relational outcomes
secular.author: Mark Regnerus and the sociology of modern sexuality
secular.whatItGetsRight: Sociological research has tracked the actual outcomes of the sexual revolution with uncomfortable candor, documenting the loneliness, the lowered relationship satisfaction, the diminished trust, and the difficulty forming lasting bonds that have followed the spread of casual sex and the unbundling of intimacy from commitment. The data suggests that the promise of free, meaningful sex without covenant has not delivered, and that the people most immersed in it are often the least satisfied and the most alone.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: This is the bill for the lie, arriving as statistics. Scripture predicted the desert, warning that sexual sin is a sin against one's own body and that the one-flesh union cannot be had cheaply without cost to the self. But sociology can only count the wreckage and correlate the variables, describing the loneliness without being able to heal it. Scripture names both the disease and the cure, that sex was made for covenant and that the human heart was made for a self-giving love it cannot find by taking. The research can show that the revolution failed. Only the gospel can offer what it failed to deliver, a love that does not consume the beloved but gives itself away.

secular.source: The case for the goodness of embodied sexuality
secular.author: Esther Perel and the modern study of desire and intimacy
secular.whatItGetsRight: Perel writes with rare honesty about desire as a real and important force, refusing the puritanism that would reduce sex to mere function or duty, and insisting that erotic life matters to human flourishing, that long-term partners must tend desire rather than assume it, and that intimacy is a living thing requiring attention, mystery, and care. She takes pleasure seriously and refuses to treat the body's longings as embarrassing.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Here Scripture and the honest secular observer agree against the prude, for the Song of Songs takes desire every bit as seriously as Perel does and celebrates it without apology. The Bible is no enemy of erotic delight, commanding husband and wife to find genuine joy in each other and refusing to treat the marriage bed as a grim duty. But Perel locates the meaning of desire largely in the self and its fulfillment, in keeping eros alive for the sake of a flourishing life, which leaves desire without a covenant to anchor it and a self at the center. Scripture honors the same desire and gives it a home, the lifelong covenant in which alone the self-giving the body enacts can be safely complete. Perel rightly defends the fire. Scripture builds the hearth that keeps it from burning down the house.

secular.source: The research on singleness, celibacy, and human flourishing
secular.author: The social science of unmarried adults and chosen celibacy
secular.whatItGetsRight: A body of research has challenged the assumption that sexual activity is essential to a fulfilled human life, documenting that the unmarried and the celibate can and do flourish, that deep friendship and community and meaningful vocation sustain a good life apart from a sexual partner, and that the cultural insistence that no one can be whole without sex is neither true nor kind to the many who, by circumstance or choice, live without it.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Scripture said this with a force the culture has forgotten, for both Jesus and Paul were unmarried, and Paul called singleness a gift and in some seasons a preferable one, freeing a person for undivided devotion to the Lord. The Bible flatly denies the cultural dogma that sex is necessary to a complete human life, holding up the celibate Christ as the most fully human person who ever lived. But the research can only show that the single can flourish, while Scripture goes further and gives the unmarried life a positive vocation and an eternal horizon, a present devotion and a future in which, Jesus says, there is no marrying, because the reality marriage only pointed at will have fully come. The studies can defend the dignity of singleness. Scripture can make it a calling.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who hold the same Bible and the same conviction that sex belongs within the marriage covenant still differ on how the church should pastor people toward that vision, and the difference is not careless. It runs to the question of emphasis, whether the recovery of the body's goodness most needs a clear and bracing call to chastity or a tender and patient ministry of grace to the wounded. Hear each view at its strongest, because both love the same gift, and both are guarding against a real danger.

views.view: The clear call to chastity and the dignity of the boundary
views.body: This view holds that the most loving thing the church can offer a confused and wounded generation is clarity, a frank, unembarrassed, and unflinching presentation of the biblical vision, that sex belongs within the lifelong covenant of marriage and that chastity outside it and faithfulness within it are not arbitrary rules but the very shape of love. The danger this view guards against is a false compassion that, in its eagerness not to wound, withholds the truth that alone can heal, leaving people to discover the cost of the lie on their own in the wreckage of their lives. Advocates of this view argue that the culture is drowning precisely because no one will tell it the truth about the body, that the church's embarrassed silence has been a failure of love, and that a clear and confident call to chastity, far from being harsh, is the kindest gift the church can give the children of the sexual revolution. They will tell you that boundaries are not the enemy of desire but its protection, that the fence around the fire is what keeps it warming the house rather than burning it down. But hear the steelman clearly. This view insists that the call to chastity must be spoken with the very grace Jesus showed the woman he refused to condemn, never with shame and never with the self-righteousness that breaks a bruised reed, and the careful advocate knows that truth delivered without tenderness has wounded as many as silence ever did.

views.view: The patient ministry of grace to the wounded and the longing
views.body: This view holds that most people in the pews are not in need of clearer rules, which they already know, but of grace, having already been wounded by sexual sin, by shame, by abuse, by the long ache of unmet longing, and that the church's first word to them must be the mercy of Jesus who did not condemn. The danger this view guards against is a cold orthodoxy that knows the right answers about the body and crushes actual people with them, that has driven the broken and the struggling out of the church by meeting their wounds with condemnation rather than with the kindness that leads to repentance. Advocates of this view argue that the culture is full of people the church has already shamed, the divorced, the addicted, the single and aching, the survivors of abuse, and that they will never hear the truth about the body's goodness from a church that has nothing for them but a finger pointed at their failure. They will tell you that Jesus reached the woman at the well and the woman caught in adultery through mercy first, and that grace, not law, is what finally reorders a disordered desire. But hear the steelman clearly. This view insists that grace is not the abandonment of the truth but the only soil in which the truth can take root, that mercy must finally say with Jesus go and sin no more, and the careful advocate knows that a compassion which never calls anyone toward the goodness of chastity has not loved them but only left them in the desert.

parts.title: What Chastity Forms in a Person
parts.body:
You will not white-knuckle your way to a rightly ordered desire. I have known the biblical vision of the body for decades, and the knowing has never once, by itself, governed a single appetite, because desire is not a belief to be corrected but a power to be reordered, and it is reordered not by the mere force of will but by the slow reshaping of what a person actually loves. Chastity, rightly understood, is not the suppression of desire but its redemption, and along the way God forms specific things in the one who walks the long path, things that neither the prude nor the libertine ever receives.

He forms reverence, the recovery of the body as holy. The culture trains us to see bodies as objects, our own and others, things to be used or improved or consumed, and chastity slowly retrains the eye to see a person where the culture sees a body, a beloved made in the image of God where the appetite saw only an object of desire. This is not the prude's flinching from the body but its opposite, a reverence so deep that the body becomes too meaningful to waste, too holy to consume. The chaste person is not the one who has killed desire. It is the one who has learned to see the temple and not merely the flesh.

He forms self-giving, the very heart of love, because the deepest thing wrong with disordered desire is that it takes rather than gives, and the deepest thing right with rightly ordered desire is that it pours itself out. The whole biblical vision of sex is self-gift, two persons giving themselves wholly to each other within a covenant, and chastity is the long training of a heart out of the reflex to consume and into the reflex to give. The one who learns chastity learns the love that made the universe and gave itself away, the love that does not grasp the beloved but lays itself down. This is why the chaste and the truly married are learning the same lesson, the lesson of a love that gives.

He forms patience and the strange dignity of waiting, especially for those who long. The single believer who holds desire in trust, who does not seize the counterfeit, who waits, sometimes for years, sometimes for a lifetime, is not merely enduring a deprivation. They are being formed in the deepest posture of faith, the willingness to trust God with an unmet ache, to believe that the good gift withheld is still in the hands of a good God, to hold a longing open before him rather than forcing it shut with a substitute. There is a glory in that waiting the culture cannot see, the glory of a person whose hope is set on something the present cannot give.

And he forms a desire that finally points home, which is the deepest formation of all. Every human longing for union, for intimacy, for the beloved, was always a signpost, a finite ache pointing toward an infinite fulfillment, the union with God for which the whole creation groans. The mistake of the culture is to demand that sex deliver what only God can give, to ask a finite pleasure to fill an infinite hunger, and the misery of the sexual revolution is the misery of a generation crushing the signpost trying to wring from it the destination. Chastity, rightly understood, frees desire to be what it was always meant to be, not a god that must satisfy but a sign that points, a good gift received with thanks and held with open hands, pointing past itself to the marriage of the Lamb, the union with God that every earthly longing was a rumor of all along.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: None of this is a formula, and none of it earns you anything from God, and if you carry deep wounds here, abuse, trauma, compulsion that controls you, then your first faithful step is not a checklist but help, a trusted pastor, a wise counselor, a doctor, because some of what tangles desire belongs in skilled and gentle hands and is not a willpower problem to be prayed away alone. There is no shame in that order. And if you are single and aching, hear again that your longing is not your failure and your waiting is not your punishment. Start where you are, this week, with one honest thing, and let desire be reordered slowly, the way it was disordered slowly, by grace and not by force.

steps: Break the silence with one trusted person, naming honestly whatever you have carried alone in this area, because shame lives in the dark and dies in the light, and what cannot be spoken cannot be healed.

Read the Song of Songs straight through this week, slowly and without flinching, letting it teach you that God is not ashamed of the body or the desire he made, and that the prudery you may have inherited was never from him.

If the screen has a grip on you, take one concrete protective step this week, a filter, an accountability partner, a device left in another room, treating the habit not as an embarrassment to hide but as a wound to bring into the open and begin to heal.
Practice seeing one person this week as a person and not a body, a beloved made in the image of God rather than an object of appetite, beginning the slow retraining of the eye that chastity requires.

Name your own story honestly to a trusted friend or counselor, the messages you absorbed about the body, the wounds, the habits, the shame, because the story is shaping your desire until you bring it into the light and let grace begin to rewrite it.

If you are married, have one honest and tender conversation with your spouse about the marriage bed, refusing both the prudery that cannot speak of it and the neglect that lets it grow cold, tending the good gift rather than assuming it.

Build real structures around the screen if it has held you, not relying on willpower alone but changing your environment, your devices, your accountability, because a compulsion is broken by grace working through means and not by resolve repeated and broken.

If you are single, refuse the lie that your life is on hold, investing this month in deep friendship, community, and vocation, the real goods that sustain a flourishing life, and bring your longing honestly to God rather than forcing it shut with a counterfeit.

Pursue the redemption of desire and not merely the suppression of it, asking God this season not only to help you say no to the counterfeit but to reorder your heart toward the love it was made for, because chastity is the healing of desire, not its execution.

Recover a theology of the body for yourself, reading deeply on the goodness of creation, the meaning of the one-flesh union, and the dignity of the body, until the suspicion you may have inherited gives way to the reverence Scripture actually teaches.

If wounds run deep, abuse, addiction, trauma, commit this season to skilled and gentle help, a counselor who knows this terrain, treating the seeking of that help as an act of faith and not a failure of it, because some healing requires hands more skilled than your own.

Examine where you have asked a finite pleasure to fill an infinite hunger, where you have demanded that intimacy or its counterfeit deliver what only God can give, and begin the slow work of letting desire point home rather than collapse the signpost trying to wring the destination from it.

Make the reverence for the body a settled posture of a lifetime, learning over years to see persons rather than objects, to honor the temple rather than consume the flesh, until the chaste eye and the loving heart have become simply the way you see.

Whether married or single, learn the love that gives rather than takes, the self-giving the body was always meant to enact, letting chastity school you over a lifetime into the love that made the universe and laid itself down rather than grasping.

Disciple the next generation honestly about the body, refusing the embarrassed silence that handed your own formation over to the screen and the schoolyard, telling your children the truth that the body is good, that desire means something, and that it was made to point home.

Let every earthly longing point you, over the long arc of your life, toward the union it was always a sign of, the marriage of the Lamb, the fulfillment in God for which the whole creation groans, so that desire becomes not a god that must satisfy but a faithful signpost, held with open hands, pointing past itself to the love that will finally satisfy it all.
